about: Oldest graves, gravestones, churchyards, cemeteries and notable graves of the isles (research track, 2026-10-22), each with the age claim, how secure it is, and sources with exact quotes (checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check).

entries.name: Red Lady of Paviland
entries.museum: Oxford University Museum of Natural History
entries.claim: oldest known ceremonial burial of a modern human in Western Europe
entries.evidence: Radiocarbon dates on the skeleton (revised 2009 and 2010) put it at about 34,000 years old; the 'Lady' is in fact a young man. The museum that holds the bones states the claim.

sources.title: The Red Lady of Paviland
sources.author: Oxford University Museum of Natural History
sources.quote: the most recent radiocarbon dating indicates that they are around 34,000 years old, making this the oldest known ceremonial burial of an anatomically modern human anywhere in Western Europe

sources.title: Wikipedia: Red Lady of Paviland
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A later 2010 study revised this to around 34,000 years ago

entries.name: Aveline's Hole cemetery
entries.museum: University of Bristol Spelaeological Society (surviving remains)
entries.claim: earliest scientifically dated cemetery in Britain
entries.evidence: Radiocarbon dates on the human remains (Schulting 2005) give about 10,200–10,400 years ago; much of the collection was destroyed in the Blitz. Scheduled monument NHLE 1010297.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aveline's Hole
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest scientifically dated cemetery in Britain, 10,200 and 10,400 years old, was found at Aveline's Hole

sources.title: Cheddar Man: Mesolithic Britain's blue-eyed boy
sources.author: Natural History Museum
sources.quote: Aveline's Hole which is one of the biggest Mesolithic cemeteries in Britain

entries.name: Cheddar Man, Gough's Cave
entries.claim: oldest almost complete modern human skeleton found in Britain
entries.evidence: Radiocarbon dated to about 10,000 years ago; found alone in 1903 and it is not certain he was deliberately buried, so the record is as oldest near-complete skeleton rather than oldest grave.

sources.title: Cheddar Man: Mesolithic Britain's blue-eyed boy
sources.author: Natural History Museum
sources.quote: Cheddar Man lived around 10,000 years ago and is the oldest almost complete skeleton of our species

sources.title: Cheddar Man: Mesolithic Britain's blue-eyed boy
sources.author: Natural History Museum
sources.quote: it wasn't clear whether he had been buried

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gough's Cave
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He is Britain's oldest complete human skeleton

entries.name: Hermitage Mesolithic burial
entries.location: Hermitage, near Castleconnell, Co. Limerick (coordinates of Castleconnell; site on the Shannon nearby)
entries.claim: earliest known human burial in Ireland
entries.evidence: Radiocarbon-dated cremation burials found on a bend of the Shannon in 2001 (Collins and Coyne); the adze with them is the earliest securely dated polished axe in Europe. Only a reference source was checked here.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Irish Mesolithic
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest known human burial in Ireland is dated to 7530-7320 BCE

entries.name: La Hougue Bie passage grave
entries.claim: oldest burial monument of the Channel Islands, one of the largest and best preserved passage graves in Western Europe
entries.evidence: Neolithic passage grave with a 20 m passage, excavated by the Société Jersiaise in 1925; dated to about 4000–3500 BC.

sources.title: Wikipedia: La Hougue Bie
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: La Hougue Bie is a Neolithic ritual site which was in use around 4000-3500 BC

sources.title: Wikipedia: La Hougue Bie
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: one of the largest and best preserved passage graves

entries.name: Poulnabrone portal tomb
entries.claim: one of the earliest radiocarbon-dated burials in an Irish megalithic tomb
entries.evidence: Remains of about 30 people from the 1986–88 excavation (Lynch) were radiocarbon dated to burials over some 600 years from about 3800 BC.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Poulnabrone dolmen
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The human remains and objects are estimated to have been buried intermittently during the 600-year period between 3800 and 3200 BC

entries.name: Carrowmore megalithic cemetery
entries.claim: largest and oldest group of Neolithic (megalithic) tombs in Ireland
entries.evidence: The OPW describes Carrowmore as Ireland's oldest megalithic tombs, about 6,000 years old; earlier excavator dates in the 5th millennium BC are disputed, so the safer date is the 4th millennium BC.

sources.title: Carrowmore Megalithic Cemetery
sources.author: Heritage Ireland (OPW)
sources.quote: It is the largest and oldest collection of Neolithic tombs in Ireland

sources.title: Wikipedia: Carrowmore
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: They were built in the 4th millennium BC, during the Neolithic

entries.name: Amesbury Archer
entries.claim: richest Early Bronze Age grave in Britain, with the earliest gold found in Britain
entries.evidence: Excavated by Wessex Archaeology in May 2002; radiocarbon dated to about 2300 BC; about 100 objects including gold hair ornaments dated as early as 2470 BC.

sources.title: The Amesbury Archer
sources.author: Wessex Archaeology
sources.quote: His grave was the richest ever found dating from the early Bronze Age found in Britain

sources.title: The Amesbury Archer
sources.author: Wessex Archaeology
sources.quote: The gold dated to as early as 2,470BC and is the earliest found in Britain

entries.name: Bush Barrow
entries.location: Normanton Down, Wilsford cum Lake, Wiltshire
entries.age_text: c. 1950 BC (Early Bronze Age, Wessex culture)
entries.claim: richest Bronze Age burial of the Stonehenge landscape
entries.evidence: Dug by William Cunnington in 1808; dated by its grave goods (gold lozenge, daggers, mace) to about 1950 BC.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bush Barrow
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The items date the burial to the early Bronze Age, circa 1950 BC

entries.name: Prittlewell princely burial
entries.claim: earliest dated Anglo-Saxon princely chamber grave, with Christian gold-foil crosses
entries.evidence: Found by MOLA in 2003; radiocarbon dating puts the chamber between 575 and 605, earlier than Sutton Hoo Mound 1; possibly Sæxa, brother of King Sæberht.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Prittlewell royal Anglo-Saxon burial
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Carbon dating had indicated that the tomb was built between 575 and 605

sources.title: Wikipedia: Prittlewell royal Anglo-Saxon burial
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the burial was of an early Anglo-Saxon Christian

entries.name: Sutton Hoo ship burial (Mound 1)
entries.claim: richest early Anglo-Saxon burial, probably King Rædwald of East Anglia
entries.evidence: Undisturbed ship burial excavated in 1939; coins date it to the 620s; the cemetery was used about 575–625. The identification with Rædwald is likely but not proven.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sutton Hoo
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was used in this way from around 575 to 625

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sutton Hoo
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Rædwald, the first king of the East Angles who was an actual historical figure, is the most likely person to have been buried in the ship

entries.name: Repton Viking burials
entries.location: St Wystan's churchyard and vicarage garden, Repton, Derbyshire
entries.claim: burials of the Viking Great Army's winter camp, the best dated Viking mass grave in England
entries.evidence: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle puts the army at Repton in 873–874; the Biddles' excavations (1974–88) found Viking graves and a charnel deposit of at least 249 (later 264) people, and new radiocarbon dates support a late 9th-century date.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Heathen Army
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: at the end of 873 the Vikings took up winter quarters at Repton in Derbyshire

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Heathen Army
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: revealed the disarticulated remains of at least 249 people

sources.title: Wikipedia: Repton
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A mass burial containing at least 264 individuals has been interpreted as linked to the Viking presence

entries.name: Scar boat burial
entries.claim: Viking boat grave of a man, an elderly woman and a child
entries.evidence: Rescue excavation 1991 of an eroding boat burial; dated 875–950 from grave goods and radiocarbon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Scar boat burial
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The burial, which dates to between 875 and 950 AD

entries.name: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial
entries.wikipedia_title: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial
entries.claim: first fully intact Viking boat burial found on the British mainland
entries.evidence: Excavated 2011 by the Ardnamurchan Transitions Project; dated to the 10th century by its grave goods.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is the first time a confirmable Viking boat burial has been found fully intact on the UK mainland

sources.title: Wikipedia: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Dated to the 10th century

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Tombstone of Marcus Favonius Facilis
entries.claim: one of the earliest Roman tombstones in Britain (centurion of the Twentieth Legion at Camulodunum)
entries.evidence: Facilis served with Legio XX, stationed at Colchester only between AD 43 and c. 49; the stone was erected by his freedmen and is dated by that posting and its pre-Boudican context. Find-spot coordinates approximate.

sources.title: Camulodunum
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tomb of the centurion Marcus Favonius Facilis from Rome, depicting him in full military dress, is one of the finest examples

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Tombstone of Longinus Sdapeze
entries.claim: one of the oldest Roman tombstones found in Britain
entries.evidence: Thracian cavalry officer who came with the invasion of AD 43; the tombstone is dated by the unit's presence at Camulodunum before the Boudican revolt (AD 60/61), when it was apparently thrown down. Dating is by context, not an inscribed date.

sources.title: Funerary stela of Longinus Sdapeze
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: His tombstone is one of the oldest Roman tombstones ever found in Britain

sources.title: Funerary stela of Longinus Sdapeze
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The stela was first discovered by workmen in 1928 during a site levelling project in Colchester on Lexden road

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Rufus Sita Tombstone
entries.claim: early Roman military tombstone from Glevum
entries.evidence: Thracian cavalryman of the Sixth Cohort; dated stylistically and by the early military phase at Gloucester. Find-spot coordinates approximate.

sources.title: Rufus Sita Tombstone
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a Roman soldier from the mid 1st Century AD, found near London Road, Gloucester, in 1824

sources.title: Rufus Sita Tombstone
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tombstone has been in the Gloucester City Museum & Art Gallery since 1873

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Tombstone of Regina
entries.location: Bath Street, South Shields, Tyne and Wear (find-spot, 1878)
entries.museum: Arbeia Roman Fort museum, South Shields
entries.age_text: 2nd century AD (Roman tombstone, Latin and Palmyrene)
entries.claim: best-known Roman tombstone of a woman in Britain; bilingual Latin–Aramaic
entries.evidence: Set up by Barates of Palmyra for his freed wife, a Catuvellaunian; dated to the later 2nd century from style and the fort's history. Not a claim to be the oldest, but a landmark grave marker.

sources.title: Tombstone of Regina
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tombstone was discovered in Bath Street, South Shields, in 1878

sources.title: Tombstone of Regina
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Regina's tombstone was on display in the 'Set in Stone' gallery at Arbeia Roman Fort

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Tombstone of Victor
entries.location: South Shields, Tyne and Wear (Roman cemetery; find-spot approximate)
entries.museum: Arbeia Roman Fort museum, South Shields
entries.claim: Roman tombstone of a freed Moorish slave, one of the two famous grave markers at Arbeia
entries.evidence: Erected by Numerianus of the Ala I Asturum for his freedman Victor, aged 20; dated by style and the unit's presence at South Shields.

sources.title: Arbeia
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The stone records that Victor was "of the Moorish nation"

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Tombstone of Julia Velva
entries.claim: best-preserved Roman funerary banquet tombstone from Eboracum
entries.evidence: Erected by her heir Aurelius Mercurialis; dated by style and formula. A landmark Roman grave marker rather than an 'oldest' claim.

sources.title: Tombstone of Julia Velva
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tombstone of Julia Velva was found at York on 11 July 1922 at a depth of 3.5 feet during the cutting of a road between The Mount and Southbank

sources.title: Tombstone of Julia Velva
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tomb is dated to approximately AD 210–240

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Latinus Stone
entries.claim: earliest surviving Christian memorial in Scotland
entries.evidence: Latin inscription commemorating Latinus and his daughter; dated by letter forms and formula to the mid-5th century. The claim is widely accepted. QID is for the museum where it is kept.

sources.title: Whithorn
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: includes the country's earliest surviving Christian memorial, the 5th-century inscribed Latinus Stone

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Knock y Doonee Ogham Stone
entries.location: Knock y Doonee, Andreas (find-spot, 1911; coordinates approximate)
entries.age_text: 5th or early 6th century AD (Latin and ogham memorial)
entries.claim: one of the earliest inscribed grave markers on the Isle of Man
entries.evidence: Bilingual Latin–ogham memorial to Ammecatus son of Rocatus, dated by script and formula. QID is the site. Current location is believed to be the Manx Museum (not verified here).

sources.title: Knock y Doonee Ogham Stone
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Latin and Ogham inscriptions are dated to the 5th or early 6th century, and both commemorate a person named Ammecatus son of Rocatus

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Saturninus stone, Llansadwrn
entries.claim: memorial of the church's founder Saturninus and his wife
entries.evidence: Latin inscription to 'the blessed Saturninus' and his wife, dated by formula to the 6th century. Local sites call it the oldest memorial in Wales, which is not supportable (5th-century stones exist); kept as an early named founder's grave marker.

sources.title: Llansadwrn, Anglesey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: founded in the sixth century by Saint Saturninus, who together with his wife, is commemorated by an early Christian monument

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Voteporix Stone (Castell Dwyran)
entries.claim: bilingual memorial possibly of King Vortipor of Dyfed, named by Gildas
entries.evidence: Latin MEMORIA VOTEPORIGIS PROTICTORIS with ogham VOTECORIGAS; dated by formula and script. The identification with Gildas's Vortiporius is disputed, so the 'oldest royal tombstone' claim is open.

sources.title: Vortiporius
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A memorial stone was discovered in 1895 near the church of Castell Dwyran in Carmarthenshire bearing a Christian cross and with inscriptions in both Latin and in ogham

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Penmachno consular stone (Iustini consulis)
entries.age_text: AD 540 if 'Iustinus' is the consul of 540 (otherwise 328–650)
entries.claim: the only early Christian stone in Britain dated by a consulship
entries.evidence: Fragmentary inscription read as '...son of Avitorius... in the time of Justinus the Consul'; Justinus was consul in 540 but the reading is uncertain. If correct, it is the earliest absolutely dated grave marker in the British Isles. Coordinates are the church (approximate); QID is the village.

sources.title: Penmachno
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There was a consul called Justinus in 540, but the inscription is unclear and could refer to Justus (328); the broadest date range for the slab is 328 - 650

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Lugnaedon stone, Inchagoill
entries.location: Inchagoill island, Lough Corrib, County Galway
entries.claim: oldest inscription in Ireland in the Latin alphabet
entries.evidence: Pillar inscribed LIE LUGUAEDON MACCI MENUEH ('stone of Luguaedon son of Menueh'); the 'oldest Latin-alphabet inscription' claim is traditional and the date is by letter forms only, so it is open.

sources.title: Inchagoill
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is the oldest inscription in Ireland in the Latin alphabet (all earlier inscriptions are in Ogham)

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Catamanus Stone (tombstone of King Cadfan)
entries.claim: earliest grave marker of a named, historically known king in Britain
entries.evidence: Latin inscription CATAMANUS REX SAPIENTISIMUS... to Cadfan ap Iago, king of Gwynedd (d. c. 625); dated by the king's death and letter forms. Still in the church where he was buried (QID is the church).

sources.title: St Cadwaladr's Church
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: King Cadfan ap Iago had been buried in the church, and his tombstone c. 634 is still on display today

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Hartlepool name stones
entries.location: Cross Close, Headland, Hartlepool, County Durham (find-spot, 1833 and later)
entries.museum: St Hilda's Church, Hartlepool; others in the British Museum and Durham
entries.claim: among the earliest Anglo-Saxon inscribed grave markers (from Hild's monastery, founded 640s)
entries.evidence: Small slabs with crosses and personal names in runes and Latin letters, found over burials in the cemetery of the double monastery; dated by the monastery's history and the inscriptions.

sources.title: Hartlepool Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: One of the namestones found during this excavation can be found on display in St Hilda's Church

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Kilnasaggart Pillar Stone
entries.location: Kilnasaggart, near Jonesborough, County Armagh (in situ; coordinates approximate)
entries.age_text: c. AD 700–716 (inscribed pillar over an early cemetery)
entries.claim: one of the earliest datable Christian monuments in Ireland
entries.evidence: Inscription names Ternoc son of Ciaran the Little, whose death is recorded in the annals in 714 or 716; the identification (and so the date) is probable but not certain. The pillar stands over an early Christian burial ground.

sources.title: Jonesborough, County Armagh
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The inscribed date of Ternoc's death makes this stone one of the earliest dateable Christian monuments in Ireland

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Grave slab of Gweirca ferch Owain
entries.location: Valle Crucis Abbey, near Llangollen, Denbighshire
entries.claim: earliest-dated Welsh memorial of any kind
entries.evidence: The slab's inscription ends with the year MCCLXXXX; the 'earliest-dated' claim is Peter Lord's. QID is the abbey.

sources.title: Gweirca ferch Owain
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Peter Lord states that Gweirca's grave slab is "the earliest-dated Welsh memorial of any kind"

sources.title: Gweirca ferch Owain
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: represents the earliest-dated grave slab in north Wales

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Ann Green headstone, Alstonefield
entries.claim: oldest legible (dated) gravestone in England
entries.evidence: A small circular stone inscribed with April 1518. The claim rests on local sources (parish, Wikipedia, local press) and has not been tested against a national survey; sources disagree on the day (3 or 11 April). Plausible as the earliest dated churchyard headstone, but open.

sources.title: St Peter's Church, Alstonefield
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the churchyard is a memorial stone to Ann Green, who died 11 April 1518. This is believed to be the oldest legible gravestone in England

sources.title: England's Oldest Legible Gravestone – Anne Green at St Peter's Church, Alstonefield
sources.author: Jenna Goodwin (The Red Haired Stokie), 2025
sources.quote: the gravestone of Anne Green, who died in April 1518, has survived over 500 years and remains clearly readable today

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Gibb slab, Holy Rude kirkyard, Stirling
entries.claim: oldest dated stone in Stirling's kirkyard; earlier than the 1623 Dunning stone often called Scotland's oldest
entries.evidence: Flat slab dated 1579 for a mason called Gibb (Harrison 1990, Forth Naturalist and Historian 13). It is a recumbent slab rather than an upright headstone; earlier dated medieval slabs exist in Scottish churches, so no national record is claimed.

sources.title: Stirling Holy Rude Kirk-yard
sources.author: Stirling Local History Society
sources.quote: The oldest stone identified has the date 1579. It is a flat slab and was for a stonemason called Gibb

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Rutherford stone, St Serf's, Dunning
entries.location: St Serf's churchyard, Dunning, Perth and Kinross
entries.claim: 'the oldest dated gravestone in Scotland' (local claim)
entries.evidence: The parish society's claim cites only 'one authority'; the 1579 Gibb slab at Stirling's Holy Rude is older, so the claim to be the oldest in Scotland does not hold. Kept as an early dated stone.

sources.title: St Serf's Graveyard History
sources.author: Dunning Parish Historical Society
sources.quote: The Rutherford stone dated 1623. This according to one authority is the oldest dated gravestone in Scotland

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Mac Considine tomb plaque, Ennis Friary
entries.claim: oldest fully legible gravestone in Ennis Friary
entries.evidence: Latin plaque recording that Dermot Mac Considine had the tomb made in 1631; a site claim only. The popular claim for Ireland's oldest dated headstone (Ann Dyke, Kilbrogan, Bandon, 1623) could not be checked: historicgraves.com refuses scripted access.

sources.title: Dermot Mac Considine
sources.author: Heritage Ireland (OPW)
sources.quote: This is the oldest fully legible gravestone in the friary

sources.title: Dermot Mac Considine
sources.author: Heritage Ireland (OPW)
sources.quote: LVM FIERI FECIT ANNO 1631

entries.category: Oldest dated gravestone or grave marker
entries.name: Slate headstone dated 1631, Teversal
entries.claim: one of the two earliest slate headstones in Nottinghamshire
entries.evidence: Recorded in the Nottinghamshire HER from Pevsner; a county-level claim for the slate headstone tradition of the East Midlands.

sources.title: Building record M17299 - Headstone dated 1631, St Katherine's Churchyard
sources.author: Nottinghamshire Historic Environment Record
sources.quote: In the churchyard, two of the earliest slate headstones in the county, one dated 1631

entries.name: Poundbury late Roman cemetery
entries.location: Poundbury, Dorchester, Dorset (coordinates of Poundbury Hill)
entries.claim: one of the largest early Christian (late Roman) cemeteries in Britain
entries.evidence: Excavated 1966–82 (Farwell and Molleson); over 1,000 east–west graves of the 4th century, many taken as Christian.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Durnovaria
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A large late-Roman and Christian cemetery has been excavated at Poundbury just to the west of the town

entries.name: Cannington cemetery
entries.claim: late Roman to Saxon cemetery in continuous use for about 450 years
entries.evidence: Quarried away after excavation (Rahtz 1962–63); several hundred east–west graves with finds from 350–800.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cannington Camp
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a late Roman and Saxon cemetery, with several hundred E-W (Christian) graves

entries.name: Nendrum monastic graveyard
entries.location: Mahee Island, Strangford Lough, Co. Down
entries.claim: one of the oldest monastic burial grounds in Northern Ireland
entries.evidence: Medieval tradition puts its foundation by St Mochaoi in the 5th century, which is uncertain; the inner cashel holds the graveyard.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nendrum Monastery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Medieval records say it was founded in the 5th century, but this is uncertain

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nendrum Monastery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a ruined church with a sun-dial, and a graveyard

entries.name: Clonmacnoise monastic burial ground
entries.museum: Clonmacnoise visitor centre (original crosses and grave-slabs)
entries.claim: burial place of high kings of Tara and Connacht, with over 700 early Christian grave-slabs
entries.evidence: Monastery founded by St Ciarán in 544 (annals); the largest collection of early Christian grave-slabs in Europe survives here.

sources.title: Clonmacnoise
sources.author: Heritage Ireland (OPW)
sources.quote: over 700 Early Christian graveslabs

sources.title: Wikipedia: Clonmacnoise
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: founded in 544 by Saint Ciarán

sources.title: Wikipedia: Clonmacnoise
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Many of the high kings of Tara (ardrí) and of Connacht were buried here

entries.name: Reilig Odhráin, Iona
entries.claim: burial ground of 48 early kings of Scotland
entries.evidence: The graveyard around St Oran's Chapel is the traditional royal burial place, but the figure of 48 kings comes from late medieval tradition and modern scholars doubt it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: St Oran's Chapel
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The burial ground surrounding the chapel is known as Reilig Òdhrain

sources.title: Wikipedia: Iona Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Many early Scottish kings (said to be 48 in total)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Iona Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: modern scholars are sceptical of such claims

entries.name: Bardsey Island (Ynys Enlli) burial ground
entries.claim: 'Island of 20,000 saints', a holy burial place since the 6th century
entries.evidence: Bishop Deiniol's burial in 584 rests on later tradition; the 20,000 saints are legend, though early medieval graves are known from the island.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bardsey Island
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Saint Deiniol, the Bishop of Bangor, was buried on the island in 584

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bardsey Island
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A Celtic cross amidst the ruins commemorates the 20,000 saints reputed to be buried on the island

entries.name: Monks' Graveyard, Skellig Michael
entries.claim: early medieval monastic graveyard with cross-slabs
entries.evidence: The monastery was founded between the 6th and 8th centuries; its small graveyard keeps simple cross-slabs.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Skellig Michael
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Monks of the Celtic Christian tradition founded a monastery on Skellig Michael sometime between the 6th and 8th centuries

sources.title: Wikipedia: Skellig Michael
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It contains stone crosses with mostly plain

entries.name: Reefert Church burial ground, Glendalough
entries.claim: 'Righ Fearta', burial place of the kings (the O'Tooles)
entries.evidence: The church dates from about 1100; the royal burial name is tradition. The monastery was founded in the 6th century by St Kevin.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Glendalough
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The name derives from Righ Fearta, the burial place of the kings

sources.title: Wikipedia: Glendalough
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: founded in the 6th century by St Kevin

entries.name: Kirk Maughold churchyard
entries.age_text: from the 5th–7th century (keeills and early crosses)
entries.claim: possibly the Isle of Man's oldest monastic site; churchyard with three keeills and the island's largest collection of crosses
entries.evidence: Tradition puts St Maughold here in the 5th century; the early cross-slabs and keeills in the 4-acre churchyard mark the monastic burial ground.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maughold (village)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Maughold is possibly the Isle of Man's oldest

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maughold (village)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the ruins of three keills

entries.name: Greyfriars Kirkyard
entries.claim: Edinburgh's burial ground since 1562, replacing St Giles' kirkyard
entries.evidence: Royal sanction of 1562 granted the Greyfriars garden as the burgh burial ground; burials since the late 16th century.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greyfriars Kirkyard
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The kirkyard was founded in August 1562

entries.name: Velho Cemetery
entries.location: Mile End, Tower Hamlets, Greater London
entries.claim: oldest Jewish burial ground in England (and the UK), opened a year after the resettlement
entries.evidence: The Grade II list description gives the opening as 1657, one year after the Cromwellian resettlement; the lease of 1657 and the first burial are documented in the congregation's records. Earlier medieval Jewish cemeteries (pre-1290) do not survive as burial grounds.

sources.title: Velho Cemetery of the Spanish and Portuguese Jewish Congregation of London (list entry 1319658)
sources.author: Historic England via British Listed Buildings
sources.quote: The oldest Jewish burial ground in England, opened a year after the Anglo-Jewish resettlement under Oliver Cromwell

sources.title: Sephardi Velho (Old) Cemetery (London Inventory)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.quote: The Sephardi Velho (Old) Cemetery opened in 1657, the first Jewish cemetery to be established with Oliver Cromwell's approval

entries.name: Lynastown Quaker Burial Ground
entries.claim: one of the oldest, if not the oldest, Quaker burial ground in Ireland
entries.evidence: The burial register transcribed by the Craigavon Historical Society begins with William Lynas, d. 1658, buried on family land because Quakers refused parish burial. The claim is hedged by its own source; Rosenallis (Co. Laois) also claims to be the oldest in Ireland.

sources.title: Lynastown Quaker burial ground (Review vol. 6 no. 3, 1993)
sources.author: Craigavon Historical Society
sources.quote: one of the oldest, if not the oldest Quaker graveyard in Ireland

sources.title: Lynastown Quaker burial ground (Review vol. 6 no. 3, 1993)
sources.author: Craigavon Historical Society
sources.quote: when he died on 20 June 1658, Quaker principles precluded his burial by a priest in the parish graveyard

entries.name: Quaker Gardens (Bunhill Fields Quaker burial ground)
entries.claim: one of the earliest Quaker burial grounds in England, older than the main Bunhill Fields ground
entries.evidence: Burials of Quakers here began in 1661 (Holmes, The London Burial Grounds, 1896, as summarised by a local historian). Earlier Quaker burials are recorded elsewhere (Lynastown 1658, Hull 1659), so it is not the oldest overall.

sources.title: The lost burying ground of London's Quakers
sources.author: Flickering Lamps (London history blog)
sources.quote: burials of Quakers began here in 1661

entries.name: Bunhill Fields
entries.claim: the oldest and pre-eminent Nonconformist (non-churchyard) burial ground in London; oldest surviving memorial Theophilus Gale d. 1678
entries.evidence: The 1665 enclosure is recorded in the gate inscriptions (Victorian copies of the 1665/1666 wording) quoted in the Historic England register entry (Grade I). Burials before 1678 left no surviving marker.

sources.title: Bunhill Fields Burial Ground (Register of Parks and Gardens, NHLE 1001713, via Parks & Gardens UK)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: This area was enclosed by brick walls in October 1665, with gates erected in 1666

sources.title: Bunhill Fields Burial Ground (Register of Parks and Gardens, via Parks & Gardens UK)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: The oldest marked grave is that of Theophilus Gale, who died in 1678

sources.title: Bunhill Fields Burial Ground (London Inventory)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.quote: Bunhill Fields was established in 1665 and became the country's pre-eminent Nonconformist cemetery

entries.name: Old Burial Ground, Royal Hospital Chelsea
entries.wikipedia_title: Old Burial Ground, Royal Hospital Chelsea
entries.claim: an important early military cemetery (pensioners of the Royal Hospital); a candidate for the oldest military burial ground in Britain
entries.evidence: Consecrated August 1691 for the Chelsea Pensioners; c. 10,000 burials to 1854. No source found that calls it the oldest military cemetery, so that claim is left open.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Old Burial Ground (London Inventory)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.quote: The Old Burial Ground was consecrated in August 1691

sources.title: Royal Hospital Old Burial Ground (London Inventory)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.quote: it is an important military cemetery

entries.name: Alderney Road Cemetery
entries.location: Mile End, Tower Hamlets, Greater London
entries.claim: oldest Ashkenazi Jewish cemetery in the UK
entries.evidence: Opened 1697 for the Great Synagogue's Ashkenazi community, next to the Sephardi Velho ground; extended 1749.

sources.title: Sephardi Velho (Old) Cemetery (London Inventory; nearby sites)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.locator: Nearby parks and gardens: Alderney Road Cemetery
sources.quote: Alderney Road Cemetery is the oldest Ashkenazi Jewish cemetery in the UK, which opened in 1697

entries.name: Ballybough Cemetery
entries.claim: Ireland's oldest Jewish cemetery
entries.evidence: The lease of 28 October 1718 to members of the Dublin Jewish community is documented; no rival older Jewish burial ground survives in Ireland. Reference source only.

sources.title: Ballybough Cemetery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Founded in 1718, it is Ireland's oldest Jewish cemetery

entries.name: Old Calton Burial Ground
entries.claim: early non-church burial ground bought by a trades incorporation (Incorporated Trades of Calton); burial place of David Hume
entries.evidence: The Society of the Incorporated Trades of Calton bought the ground in 1718 because burial at South Leith was inconvenient. Reference source only; no 'oldest' claim attaches to it.

sources.title: Old Calton Burial Ground
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The burial ground was opened in 1718

entries.name: Plymouth Hoe Old Jews' Burial Ground
entries.claim: earliest Jewish burial ground outside London
entries.evidence: Listed Grade II in 2017 (NHLE 1448469); the list entry gives as reason for designation that it is the earliest surviving Jewish burial ground outside London. Early inscriptions are now largely eroded.

sources.title: Old Jews' Burial Ground, Lambhay Hill (list entry 1448469)
sources.author: Historic England via British Listed Buildings
sources.quote: As one of the earliest Jewish burial grounds surviving in England and the earliest outside London

entries.name: Clifton Street Cemetery (New Burying Ground)
entries.claim: Belfast's oldest surviving town cemetery (the 'New Burying Ground', replacing the Corporation churchyard)
entries.evidence: Opened March 1797 by the Belfast Charitable Society (Clifton House archives); the older Corporation churchyard closed c. 1798–1800. 'Oldest in Belfast' is not stated by the source and is left open.

sources.title: From the Archives: The New Burying Ground (today Clifton Street Cemetery) opened in March 1797
sources.author: Clifton House (Belfast Charitable Society)
sources.quote: The New Burying Ground (today Clifton Street Cemetery) opened in March 1797

entries.name: Rusholme Road Cemetery (Gartside Gardens)
entries.claim: the first cemetery in England run by a joint-stock (proprietary) company, for Dissenters
entries.evidence: The opening in 1821 is well attested (burial registers from 1821 in Manchester Archives). It is often called the first proprietary cemetery company in Britain (company formed 1820), but one study puts the first company in 1819 and the Victoria County History gives 1823, so 'first' is left open.

sources.title: Gartside Gardens
sources.author: Manchester History (manchesterhistory.net)
sources.quote: The cemetery opened in 1821 and was known as the Dissenters Burial Ground since it was used by various non-conformist groups

entries.name: Liverpool Necropolis (Low Hill General Cemetery; Grant Gardens)
entries.claim: Liverpool's first general (non-denominational) cemetery and one of the earliest commercial cemeteries in England
entries.evidence: Opened February 1825 with buildings by John Foster Jr and closed 1898; it preceded St James's Cemetery (1829). The cemetery is lost; headstones went to Everton Cemetery.

sources.title: Liverpool's vanished necropolis
sources.author: Mike Higginbottom
sources.quote: The Low Hill General Cemetery was opened in 1825

sources.title: Grant Gardens
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Necropolis opened in 1825, with buildings by John Foster Jr

entries.name: Glasgow Necropolis
entries.age_text: first interment 1832 (Jewish section); opened 1833; planned from 1828
entries.claim: one of Scotland's first planned garden cemeteries; the first planned cemetery in Glasgow
entries.evidence: The HES Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes (GDL00366) records it as begun in 1828 with the first interment in 1832. HES says 'one of' Scotland's first, not the first.

sources.title: The Necropolis (Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes GDL00366)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: the Necropolis is one of Scotland's first planned garden cemeteries created in Victorian times

sources.title: The Necropolis (Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes GDL00366)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: The Necropolis was the first planned cemetery in Glasgow and was begun in 1828

sources.title: The Necropolis (Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes GDL00366)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: The first interment was made in 1832

entries.name: Glasnevin Cemetery
entries.claim: Ireland's first large non-denominational garden cemetery, founded by Daniel O'Connell
entries.evidence: Opened 21 February 1832 (first burial the next day); the earlier Goldenbridge cemetery (1829) was also founded by O'Connell's committee, so Glasnevin is the first garden cemetery rather than the first Catholic-run one. Reference source only.

sources.title: Glasnevin Cemetery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Established as a non-denominational garden cemetery by Daniel O'Connell in 1832

sources.title: Glasnevin Cemetery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: opened to the public for the first time on 21 February 1832

entries.name: Kensal Green Cemetery
entries.claim: first of London's commercial public cemeteries (the first of the 'Magnificent Seven')
entries.evidence: The Historic England register entry (Grade I, NHLE 1000817) states it was the first of London's 19th-century commercial cemeteries; the General Cemetery Company still owns it.

sources.title: Kensal Green (All Souls) Cemetery (Register of Parks and Gardens, NHLE 1000817, via Parks & Gardens UK)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Opened in 1833, Kensal Green was the first of London's C19 commercial public cemeteries to be established

sources.title: Kensal Green Cemetery (London Inventory)
sources.author: London Gardens Trust
sources.quote: Kensal Green Cemetery opened in 1833, the first commercial public cemetery to be established in London

entries.name: Key Hill Cemetery
entries.claim: Birmingham's first (earliest) public cemetery
entries.evidence: The Historic England register entry (Grade II*) dates the opening to 1836 by the Birmingham General Cemetery Company.

sources.title: Key Hill Cemetery (Register of Parks and Gardens, via Parks & Gardens UK)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Birmingham City's first cemetery, laid out by Charles Edge for the Birmingham General Cemetery Company, and opened in 1836

entries.name: Brookwood Cemetery Muslim burial ground (Plot M1)
entries.claim: Britain's first dedicated Muslim burial ground
entries.evidence: The cemetery says the Muslim plot was set up in 1884 by G. W. Leitner (founder of the Shah Jahan Mosque); the Historic England register text gives 'the 1890s'. Both agree it was the first in Britain; the exact year is uncertain (1884 vs 1890s).

sources.title: Muslim burials
sources.author: Brookwood Cemetery
sources.quote: Brookwood Cemetery is home to Britain’s first dedicated Muslim cemetery, established in 1884 by Dr. Gottlieb Wilhelm Leitner

sources.title: Brookwood Cemetery (Register of Parks and Gardens, via Parks & Gardens UK)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: The neighbouring Muslim grounds were opened in the 1890s and were the first in Britain

entries.name: Grave of St Patrick
entries.age_text: Patrick died c. 461; grave stone placed 1900
entries.claim: burial place of St Patrick
entries.evidence: The burial is a tradition; the granite slab marking the 'grave' was laid only in 1900, so the marker is modern.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Down Cathedral
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the inscribed stone of Mourne granite allegedly marking the grave was actually put in place in 1900

entries.name: St Cuthbert's coffin
entries.location: Durham Cathedral (grave behind the high altar; coffin in the cathedral treasury)
entries.claim: oldest surviving decorated wooden coffin in England
entries.evidence: The carved oak coffin was made for Cuthbert's translation at Lindisfarne in 698 and held his remains until 1827; it was taken out of the grave in 1899.

sources.title: Wikipedia: St Cuthbert's coffin
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which between AD 698 and 1827 contained the remains of Saint Cuthbert

sources.title: Wikipedia: St Cuthbert's coffin
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: probably to date to 698

entries.name: Grave of Bede
entries.age_text: died AD 735; at Durham from c. 1020, shrine 1370
entries.claim: the oldest marked grave of a named English writer
entries.evidence: Bede was buried at Jarrow in 735; his bones were taken to Durham about 1020, given a shrine in the Galilee Chapel in 1370, and reburied there after the shrine was destroyed at the Reformation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bede
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Bede died at Jarrow on the Feast of the Ascension, 26 May 735, and was buried there

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bede
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Bede's remains were moved to a shrine in the Galilee Chapel at Durham Cathedral in 1370

entries.name: Lost grave of King Alfred
entries.museum: Winchester City Museum (bones from the site)
entries.claim: burial place of Alfred the Great, lost after the Dissolution
entries.evidence: Alfred, Edward the Elder and Ealhswith were reburied at Hyde Abbey; the graves were destroyed in 1788 and the remains lost. A pelvis from the site was dated to 895–1017 in 2014 but is not proven to be Alfred's.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hyde Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Abbey was once known to have housed the remains of King Alfred the Great

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hyde Abbey
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Following its dissolution these remains were lost

entries.name: Grave of Brian Boru
entries.location: St Patrick's Cathedral (Church of Ireland), Armagh
entries.claim: burial place of the High King killed at Clontarf
entries.evidence: The annals record his burial at Armagh; the exact place in the north wall is tradition, marked by a modern plaque.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Brian Boru
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: His tomb is said to be in the north wall of St Patrick's Cathedral in the city of Armagh

entries.name: Effigy of Abbot Gilbert Crispin
entries.claim: oldest effigy in Westminster Abbey and among the earliest tomb effigies in England
entries.evidence: Black marble effigy of the abbot who died in 1117; the Abbey calls it its oldest effigy. 'Earliest in England' is not established (Exeter and Salisbury have rivals).

sources.title: Gilbert Crispin
sources.author: Westminster Abbey
sources.quote: This is the oldest effigy at the Abbey

entries.name: Tomb of King John
entries.claim: oldest royal effigy in England
entries.evidence: John was buried at Worcester in 1216; the Purbeck marble effigy was made in 1232 and the tomb chest about 1529–40.

sources.title: King John
sources.author: Worcester Cathedral
sources.quote: has the oldest royal effigy in England

sources.title: Wikipedia: John, King of England
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A new sarcophagus with an effigy was made for him in 1232

entries.name: Effigy of Robert Curthose
entries.claim: rare 13th-century wooden (bog oak) tomb effigy
entries.evidence: The carved oak effigy is about a century later than the duke's death; the mortuary chest is much later.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robert Curthose
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: His effigy carved in bog oak

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robert Curthose
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The effigy dates from about 100 years after his death

entries.name: Stone coffin of Llywelyn the Great
entries.location: Gwydir Chapel, St Grwst's Church, Llanrwst, Conwy
entries.claim: coffin of the Prince of Gwynedd, moved from Aberconwy Abbey
entries.evidence: Llywelyn was buried at Aberconwy in 1240; the stone coffin was moved to Maenan and then Llanrwst after the Dissolution. The body is lost.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Llywelyn the Great
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Llywelyn's stone coffin can now be seen in St Grwst's Church, Llanrwst

entries.name: Temple Church effigies
entries.claim: among the earliest knightly effigies in England (incl. William Marshal)
entries.evidence: Nine stone effigies of the 13th and 14th centuries, badly damaged in 1941 and restored; 'earliest' is a common but loosely sourced claim.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Temple Church
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: its 13th- and 14th-century stone effigies

entries.name: Shrine of Edward the Confessor
entries.claim: oldest royal burial still in its shrine in Britain
entries.evidence: Henry III's translation of 13 October 1269 put the body in the shrine where it still lies.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Edward the Confessor
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: remains where it was after the final translation of his body to a chapel east of the sanctuary on 13 October 1269

entries.name: Tomb of Robert the Bruce
entries.claim: grave of Robert I, rediscovered in 1818
entries.evidence: The king's vault was found in 1818 during building of the new parish church and the skeleton examined; his heart is at Melrose.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robert the Bruce
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Robert's body is buried in Dunfermline Abbey

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robert the Bruce
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On 17 February 1818, workmen breaking ground on the new parish church

entries.name: Grave of Richard III
entries.wikipedia_title: Exhumation and reburial of Richard III of England
entries.location: Leicester Cathedral (first grave: Greyfriars friary site, Leicester)
entries.claim: the lost grave of the last Plantagenet king, found in 2012
entries.evidence: The skeleton found at Greyfriars in 2012 was identified by DNA, radiocarbon and osteology and reburied in the cathedral on 26 March 2015.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
